rejected.title: Consumer guarantees
card: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL) gives consumers automatic rights, called consumer guarantees, when they buy goods. No store policy or sign can take them away, and the buyer does not pay extra for them.
Acceptable quality
Goods must be safe, work properly, last a reasonable time, look right and do what such goods are normally used for, given the price and what they are.
Fit for purpose
Goods must suit any particular purpose the buyer told the seller about, or that the seller said they would suit.
Match description
Goods must match what the seller said, or what the label, packaging, sample or advertisement showed.
rejected.remember: Quality, purpose and description: three guarantees that no store policy can remove.

a.q: Zoe buys a new kettle in Newcastle. She tells the seller nothing special about how she will use it. It stops working after two days. Which consumer guarantee is most clearly broken?
opts: Acceptable quality, because it failed far too soon
Match description, because it was not advertised
Fit for purpose, because kettles are for boiling water
None, because the store gave no written warranty
a.why: A new kettle should work properly, do its normal job and last a reasonable time, so the guarantee of acceptable quality is broken. Fit for purpose is about a particular purpose the buyer told the seller about, and Zoe named none. A written warranty is not needed, because the guarantees apply automatically.
a.clue: Which guarantee covers what goods are normally used for?

b.q: Sam buys a tent in Orange. A sign on the shop wall says no refunds on camping gear. The tent leaks in light rain, though its label says waterproof. What is the position?
opts: The sign cannot remove the match description guarantee
The sign is valid, because Sam saw it before buying
The guarantees apply only if Sam paid for extra cover
The guarantees are void, as camping gear is used outdoors
b.why: The tent does not match its description, as the label said waterproof. Consumer guarantees apply whatever the store's own policy says, so a no refunds sign cannot take them away. Seeing the sign before buying does not change this.
b.clue: Does a store's own sign override the law?

draft.title: Consumer guarantees
card: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL) gives consumers automatic rights when they buy goods. These rights are called consumer guarantees. The business does not have to offer them and the buyer does not have to pay extra.
Acceptable quality
Goods must be safe, work properly, last a reasonable time and look right, given the price and what they are.
Fit for purpose
Goods must do what they are normally used for, and any particular job the buyer told the seller about.
Match description
Goods must match what the seller said, or what the label, packaging, sample or advertisement showed.
draft.remember: Goods must be of acceptable quality, fit for purpose and match their description, whatever the store's policy says.

problems.detail: The card says 'fit for purpose' covers what goods are normally used for. Under the ACL, being fit for the purposes goods are commonly supplied for is part of acceptable quality (s54). Fit for purpose (s55) covers a particular purpose the buyer made known, or that the business said the goods would be fit for. This overlap also makes the kettle in question a seem to break fit for purpose under the card's own definition.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations agree with the card. The card's definition of 'fit for purpose' wrongly includes normal use, which the ACL places under acceptable quality, so it should be limited to a purpose the buyer told the seller about or the seller promised.
